prompt: `String name = "ana"; name.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(name);` What does it print?
hint: What did the first call do with its result?

choices.text: `ANA`, because `toUpperCase` changes the string it is called on
choices.why: No method of `String` changes the string; this one returned a new one that nobody kept.

choices.text: `ana`
choices.why: Right: the capitals were in a new string that was thrown away, and `name` still points at `"ana"`.

choices.text: Nothing: the line does not compile, since the result is ignored
choices.why: Ignoring a result compiles without a word; that is what makes the bug easy to write.

prompt: `a` is the literal `"java"` and `c` was built at run time with a `StringBuilder`. Why does `a == c` print `false`?

choices.text: The characters differ in a way `println` does not show, such as a hidden space
choices.why: `a.equals(c)` printed `true`: the characters are identical.

choices.text: `==` asks whether they are the same object, and `c` is a new one
choices.why: Right: same text, two objects, and `==` compares references.

choices.text: A `StringBuilder` result is not a real `String` until `intern()` is called
choices.why: `toString()` returns an ordinary `String`; `intern()` only finds the shared copy.

choices.text: `==` compares lengths, and the builder added a terminating character
choices.why: `==` on objects compares references, and both strings have four characters.

prompt: A program reads a command from the keyboard into `cmd` and checks `if (cmd == "quit")`. In a quick test with `String cmd = "quit";` written in the code, it worked. What happens with real input?
hint: Where does a string typed by a person come from?

choices.text: It works the same, because both hold the text `quit`
choices.why: Same text, but `==` does not compare text; the typed string is a different object.

choices.text: The test is false even when the person types `quit`
choices.why: Right: input is built at run time, a new object, so `==` with the literal fails; `equals` is the fix.

choices.text: It fails to compile, since `==` is not allowed between strings
choices.why: It compiles: `==` is legal on any two references, which is why the bug survives.

choices.text: It throws a `NullPointerException` the first time
choices.why: Nothing is null here; `==` just answers `false`.

prompt: A string literal that spans several lines and opens with three double quotes is called a text ___.
`s` is `"Machado de Assis;Dom Casmurro;1899"`. What does `s.substring(0, s.indexOf(';'))` return?

choices.text: `Machado de Assis`
choices.why: Right: from 0 up to but not including 16, the position of the `;`.

choices.text: `Machado de Assis;`
choices.why: That would include index 16; `substring` stops before its second index.

choices.text: `achado de Assis`
choices.why: Positions start at 0, so index 0 is the `M`.
That is what `indexOf` returns; `substring` returns text.

prompt: `"Zebra".compareTo("apple")` printed `-7`. Sorting `Zebra`, `apple` and `banana` with `compareTo`, which comes first?
hint: A negative result means the left one sorts first.

choices.text: `apple`, because A is the first letter of the alphabet
choices.why: That is a person's order; `compareTo` compares character codes, and capitals come before small letters.

choices.text: `Zebra`
choices.why: Right: every capital has a smaller code than every small letter, so `Z` sorts before `a`.

choices.text: `banana`, because it is the longest
choices.why: Length decides only when one string is the start of the other.

prompt: A program checks `command.toUpperCase().equals("TITLE")`, with no locale. It passes every test in Brazil and fails on a customer's machine in Istanbul. What fixes it?

choices.text: Use `equalsIgnoreCase` on the result of `toUpperCase()`
choices.why: The result is already `TİTLE`, with a dotted capital, which no case rule turns into `I`.

choices.text: Call `strip()` first, since the Turkish keyboard adds spaces
choices.why: Nothing about spaces here: the upper-casing itself changed the letter.

choices.text: Pass `Locale.ROOT` as the argument, as for any identifier
choices.why: Right: without an argument the machine's language is used, and in Turkish `i` becomes `İ`.

choices.text: Compare with `==` instead of `equals`
choices.why: `==` compares references and would fail everywhere, not only in Turkey.

prompt: A string holds one thumbs-up emoji and nothing else. What does its `length()` return?
Why is `s = s + "x"` slow inside a loop that runs 50,000 times?

choices.text: Because `+` converts `"x"` into a number and back each time
choices.why: `"x"` is already text; nothing is converted.

choices.text: Every step builds a new string and copies all the old characters into it
choices.why: Right: the copies grow with the string, so the total grows with the square of the length.

choices.text: Because the JIT compiler cannot compile a loop that contains a `String`
choices.why: The JIT compiles such loops; the work is in the copying, compiled or not.

choices.text: Because every `+` writes the string to disk
choices.why: Nothing touches the disk; it is all memory and copying.

prompt: In the run the section quotes, the `+` loop took 1715 ms and the `StringBuilder` loop 5 ms. How many times as long did the `+` loop take? Give a whole number.
`javap -c` on `"Hello, " + name + ", you have " + books + " books"` showed one `invokedynamic` and no `StringBuilder`. What does that tell you?
hint: Count the calls, not the plus signs.

choices.text: That `+` outside a loop is as slow as inside one
choices.why: One expression became one call that sizes the result once; the cost is in repeating it in a loop.

choices.text: That the compiler ignored `books` because it is an `int`
choices.why: `iload_1` loaded `books`, and the greeting printed `3`.

choices.text: That the whole expression is one call, so `+` here costs nothing extra
choices.why: Right: the compiler turns the expression into one `makeConcatWithConstants` call.

prompt: Where does the section's rule say to reach for a `StringBuilder`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A loop that appends one line per book to a report string
choices.why: Yes: one string growing inside a loop is the case it exists for.

choices.text: A single `return "Hello, " + name;` in a method
choices.why: One expression is one call; `+` is clearer and costs nothing extra.

choices.text: Building a 10,000-character line one character at a time
choices.why: Yes: each `+` would copy everything so far.

choices.text: Joining a title and an author for one `println`
choices.why: Outside a loop, `+` is the clearer choice.

prompt: Which placeholder prints `12.5` as `12.50`?

choices.why: `%d` is for whole numbers, and a `double` makes it throw.
A width of 2 for a whole number; it says nothing about decimal places.
Right: `.2` is the number of places after the point.
`%s` prints the value as text, `12.5`, with no padding of decimals.

prompt: Match each format with what it printed in `Format.java`.
`String.format("%d copies", "three")` compiled. What happened when it ran?
hint: The compiler sees the format as a plain string.

choices.text: It printed `three copies`
choices.why: `%d` takes whole numbers only; it does not fall back to text.

choices.text: It printed `0 copies`, the default for a value that is not a number
choices.why: No default is substituted; the call fails.

choices.text: It threw `IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.String`
choices.why: Right: the mismatch is found only when the line runs, and the program ended with status 1.

prompt: A program writes prices into a CSV file that another program reads. It uses `String.format("%.2f", price)` and runs on a server set to `pt-BR`. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
hint: Which locale does `String.format` use without one?

choices.text: Prices come out as `12,50`, and the reader expecting a point misreads them; pass `Locale.ROOT`
choices.why: Right: text for another program takes `Locale.ROOT`, so it is the same on every machine.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong: `%.2f` always writes a point
choices.why: Without a locale, the machine's default decides, and in `pt-BR` that is a comma.

choices.text: The format throws on a Brazilian machine; use `%s` instead
choices.why: It does not throw. And `%s` would print every digit of the `double`, which is a different problem.

prompt: Which of these lines leaves `title` holding capitals afterwards?
hint: A method returns; an assignment keeps.

choices.text: `title.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);`
choices.why: The result is returned and dropped; `title` is unchanged.

choices.text: `title = title.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);`
choices.why: Right: the new string is assigned back to the variable.

choices.text: `String upper = title.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);`
choices.why: This keeps the capitals in `upper`, and `title` still holds the original.

choices.text: `title.equals(title.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));`
choices.why: This only compares the two; nothing is assigned.

prompt: Put these steps in the order a program follows to turn `"  Machado de Assis;Dom Casmurro;1899  "` into the year as text.
A report loop does `report = report + String.format("%s: %d%n", title, copies);` for 20,000 books, and it is slow. What change fixes the speed without changing the output?

choices.text: Replace `String.format` with `+` inside the loop, since `+` compiles to a single call
choices.why: The format call is not the problem; the growing `report` copied on every pass is.

choices.text: Call `report.intern()` after the loop
choices.why: `intern` finds a shared copy; it does nothing about the copies already made.

choices.text: Append each formatted line to one `StringBuilder` and call `toString()` once at the end
choices.why: Right: the builder grows in place, and only the final string is copied.

choices.text: Use `%s` for `copies` instead of `%d`
choices.why: The placeholder changes nothing about speed; the copying does.
